about: First-year student who drafts quickly and revises the night before. Her instructors keep flagging the same two things: an opening that announces a topic instead of making a claim, and comma splices. She wants help planning and catching grammar, but no one else's sentences in her essays, and she submits her own work.

assistant_rules.note: Help me plan and point out grammar fixes as suggestions I can accept or reject. Don't write or rewrite my sentences. I submit my own work.

messages.author: instructor
messages.text: Welcome to English 110. You may use AI tools to plan and organize your work and to talk through your drafts, but not to suggest or write wording. Ask me if you are unsure.

messages.author: student
messages.text: Can I use an AI tool to turn your comments into a checklist?

messages.author: instructor
messages.text: Yes, that is planning. The sentences in the essay have to be yours.

messages.author: instructor
messages.text: AI tools may help with planning and with grammar or wording suggestions that you review yourself. The ideas and the argument must be yours.

assignments.title: Essay 1: A place that taught you something
assignments.prompt: Write about a place that taught you something, and make a claim about what it taught you. About 600 words.

paragraphs: p1
This essay is about my grandmother's kitchen in Kochi and what I learned there. Every summer I spent three weeks with her, and most of each day happened in that kitchen.
p2

She cooked for twelve people without a recipe, she measured salt with the palm of her hand. When I asked how she knew it was enough, she said the food would tell me. I thought she was joking until I burned my first batch of appam.
p3
Now I cook in a dorm kitchen with a timer and a phone. I still taste before I measure. Her kitchen taught me that paying attention is a skill you can practise.

comments.quote: This essay is about my grandmother's kitchen in Kochi and what I learned there.
comments.text: This tells me the topic, not what you learned. Your last sentence holds the real claim; could the essay start from it?

replies.author: student
replies.text: Thanks, I'll start from the claim next time.

comments.text: Comma splice: two complete sentences joined by a comma.

assignments.title: Response paper 1: Sugar and the Atlantic economy
assignments.prompt: Using the course readings, explain why sugar became central to the Atlantic economy. About 500 words.

paragraphs: p1
In this paper I will discuss the reasons sugar became important in the Atlantic world. There were many reasons, including European demand, Caribbean land and the slave trade.
p2

Demand in Europe grew quickly in the seventeenth century, sugar went from a luxury to an everyday food. Planters in Barbados and Jamaica cleared land for cane, and they forced enslaved Africans to do the work.
p3
Mintz argues that sugar changed what working people in England ate. Taken together, these reasons explain why sugar mattered so much.

comments.quote: In this paper I will discuss the reasons sugar became important in the Atlantic world.
comments.text: You list causes but you do not argue. Which one mattered most, and why?

comments.quote: in the seventeenth century, sugar went

comments.text: Good use of the reading. Give the page number.

assignments.title: Essay 2: Should our city make buses free?
assignments.prompt: Take a position on a local policy question, argue for it and answer at least one objection. About 1,000 words in the final essay; bring a 400-word draft to peer review.

paragraphs: p1

Last month the city council debated whether to make the 14 and 22 bus lines free for riders. Supporters packed the meeting, and so did a few business owners who were worried about the cost. This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not. Most mornings the bus is full before it reaches the hospital stop.
p2

Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think, a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week. A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.
p3

The main objection is cost. Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere. This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it. Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, I do not think that is true. Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.
p4

Free buses would also help the environment. More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon. On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light. The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour. Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street. Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.
p5

In conclusion, there are good arguments on both sides. Free buses cost money, but so do cars, parking and missed shifts. Students, nurses and part-time workers would feel the difference first. I think the city should try free buses on the 14 and 22 for one year and count who rides. If ridership grows the way it did in Riverton, the council will have its answer.

comments.quote: This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate.
comments.text: This announces a topic again, as in Essay 1. What do you want the council to do, and why? Your conclusion already has the answer.
By how much, and how do you know? Name the source.
You name the objection but never answer it. Where would the money come from?

comments.quote: there are good arguments on both sides
comments.text: Here is your real position: a one-year trial. Lead with it in the first paragraph.

comments.quote: Free buses would also help the environment.
comments.text: This feels like a new topic. How does it connect to the fare argument?
I'm not sure what 'respectful' means here. Did someone actually say this?

comments.quote: most people think, a monthly pass
comments.text: Comma splice: these are two sentences. Try a period or a semicolon.
Another comma splice, the same pattern as in paragraph 2.

comments.quote: Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.
comments.text: The last sentence raises a new problem. Develop it or cut it.
